claim: Only the Palestinians became refugees in 1948.

heard.who: Yated Ne'eman, an anti-Zionist ultra-Orthodox Israeli newspaper, quoted by Yehouda Shenhav
heard.quote: this talk about 'Jewish refugees who were expelled from Arab countries' as opposed to 'Arab refugees who were expelled from the land of Israel' was grating to our journalistic ears

heard.who: Shlomo Hillel, Israeli minister and organiser of the Iraqi Jews' departure, quoted by Yehouda Shenhav (1998)
heard.quote: I do not regard the exodus of Jews from Arab countries as refugees.

answer: Palestinians were not the only people displaced in these years. About 800,000 Jews are estimated to have lived in Arab countries around 1948, and most left over the next two decades, many to Israel and others to Europe and North America. Reasons differed by country: Egypt after 1956 saw expulsions, Iraq's government let Jews leave if they gave up their citizenship, and one scholar finds a mix of push and pull in Iraq. These figures are estimates. Scholars differ on the word refugee: Shenhav calls it not unreasonable given post-war usage. The Jewish refugee claim has been used in arguments about Palestinian return and compensation; whether the two cases cancel out is an argument these facts do not settle.

contested: Numbers: the totals (800,000, 820,000, 851,000) come from encyclopedia estimates, an exhibition review, and Israeli and Jewish organisations; they are estimates, not counts of departures, and no single agreed figure exists.

The word refugee: Shlomo Hillel (quoted in Shenhav) rejects it; the ultra-Orthodox paper Yated Ne'eman said the migration was Zionist immigration and not deportation. Shenhav argues that the World Organization of Jews from Arab Countries, active from the 1970s, used the population-exchange thesis mainly to contest the Palestinian right of return.
Causes differ by country and period: Mendes finds both push and pull in Iraq; the K. review says forcible expulsion was the exception overall.
Whether the exodus was an equal 'exchange' with the Palestinian one is argued in the K. review; this card does not make that claim.
Egypt shows how far sources differ: the Gale entry gives about 100,000 Jews in 1948, the Jewish Virtual Library table 75,000, and the K. review 40,000 before 1956.

The Gale entry says the estimated 800,000 'were subjected to anti-Jewish violence, abuse, and persecution'; the K. review says forcible expulsion was the exception and most had little plan to leave. This card uses the Gale entry only for the number.
could_not_verify: An independent demographic or scholarly total for the Jewish population of Arab countries in 1948 and departures. Sergio DellaPergola's estimates exist (about 945,000 in the Middle East and North Africa in 1948 by one summary), but his papers were PDFs the checker could not read, so they are not cited.
Moshe Sicron's arrivals-by-country table is on a page I read, but it counts arrivals in Israel only, not departures, so I cited only its text on the airlifts.
A third reliable source for the 800,000 to 850,000 population figure (two reliable plus an advocacy table).
A third reliable source for the debate over the word refugee (two scholarly used; the third is advocacy and does not count).
Country-by-country breakdowns beyond Iraq and Morocco from a source other than Encyclopedia.com.
not_claimed: This card does not say Jewish displacement cancels out Palestinian displacement, or that one makes the other acceptable.
It does not claim every Jew who left an Arab country was expelled.
It does not claim the Arab states acted on one plan; it records different cases.
It does not give a settled number; all figures here are estimates.

answer_claims.says: Palestinians were not the only people displaced in these years.
About 800,000 Jews are estimated to have lived in Arab countries around 1948, and most left over the next two decades, many to Israel and others to Europe and North America.
Reasons differed by country: Egypt after 1956 saw expulsions, Iraq's government let Jews leave if they gave up their citizenship, and one scholar finds a mix of push and pull in Iraq.
Scholars differ on the word refugee: Shenhav calls it not unreasonable given post-war usage.
The Jewish refugee claim has been used in arguments about Palestinian return and compensation; whether the two cases cancel out is an argument these facts do not settle.

skeptic.notes: Read two or more sources per fact. Pro-Palestinian attack (the stronger one): every population and departure figure comes from Israeli or Jewish sources (an encyclopedia entry, an exhibition review, an advocacy table), the Gale entry says all 800,000 were 'subjected to violence' while another source on the card says expulsion was the exception, and the card has no source on Iraq 1950-51 (the dispute over who caused the bombings) or on Egypt's own figures; the 'refugee' fact rests on Shenhav alone, whose thesis is that the label was built to counter return. Pro-Israel attack: the card gives no UN or international recognition of these Jews as refugees (the UNHCR 1957 statement on Egypt is not here), no Arab League 1947 draft law against Jews, no Farhud 1941, and no denaturalisation laws, so 'expulsion and pressure' is thin; Egypt's 1956 expulsions appear only in one sentence. The heard quotes (Yated, Hillel) do not say 'only Palestinians became refugees'; they say Jews who went to Israel were not refugees. should-fix: add the strongest voice for the claim (a Palestinian-side author). must-fix: fact 0 and fact 3 have only two reliable sources (the third is the advocacy table), so the gate refuses verified; fact 3 mixes the label debate (Shenhav) with causes (Mendes); reworded. Numbers: 800,000-851,000 are estimates of population around 1948, not counts of departures; Egypt differs 100,000/75,000/40,000 across sources (added to contested). nit: the card calls Hillel an Israeli minister; the Shenhav page says only that he was active in the Iraqi Zionist underground. Independence: the K. review appears in four facts and is itself a review of one exhibition.
